nature-gov-166.title: Fortress conservation: protecting nature by removing people
nature-gov-166.text: After the United States passed its 1872 national park law, army cavalry guarded the new parks, often expelling Native Americans. That pattern became known as the Yosemite model. Fortress conservation tries to protect nature by creating reserves cut off from people. Its toll is large and uncertain. A UN special rapporteur says up to 250,000 people have been forcibly evicted for conservation since 1990. Another estimate puts displacement between 10.8 million and 173 million. Conservation charities have increasingly militarized anti-poaching work, sometimes arming paramilitary groups. Money helps drive it, through ecotourism income and carbon credits from saved forests. Many Indigenous groups have lived in forests for centuries without formal title deeds, which leaves them open to eviction. The evidence cuts against exclusion. In the Brazilian Amazon, community land titles brought less forest clearing than state-run parks, and community concessions in the Congo show less deforestation. Evicted people may end up working for extractive companies, so exclusion can increase exploitation. Some conservation leaders still argue for removing people, while Indigenous rights advocates say giving residents legal title protects forests better.

nature-gov-215.title: Indigenous land rights
nature-gov-215.text: In Brazil, only 14% of Indigenous lands ended up formally marked out under laws from 1983, and much was lost to mining companies. Indigenous land rights are the rights of Indigenous peoples, as individuals or groups, to land and the resources on it, mostly in colonized countries. Land carries religious meaning and underpins identity, self-determination and livelihoods. In some societies, the resources of land and sea are the household economy, so ownership secures access to food and income. Claims may rest on international law, treaties, common law, or national constitutions. Key international texts include a 1989 labor convention and a 2007 UN declaration, described in {{ref:nature-gov-181}} and {{ref:nature-gov-183}}. The gap between land recognized on paper and land held by custom is a major source of underdevelopment, conflict and environmental damage.

nature-gov-165.title: Green grabbing: land seized in nature's name
nature-gov-165.text: In 2008, journalist John Vidal wrote a Guardian article titled "The great green land grab." He coined a term for taking land and resources, often by foreign actors, in the name of environmental goals in ways that produce unjust development. Green grabbing is also called green colonialism. Land may be taken for ecotourism, for protecting biodiversity or ecosystem services, for carbon trading, or for biofuels. Carbon-trading firms, for instance, may take land to plant trees and sell the resulting offsets. The International Land Coalition says 59% of land grabs between 2000 and 2010 were for biofuels. Green grabs can cover thousands or millions of hectares and drive Indigenous or peasant communities off their land. Indebted governments are especially exposed, since they may sell public assets to avoid bankruptcy. Critics worry the 30 by 30 target could bring a new wave.

nature-gov-204.title: Environmental gentrification: when greening pushes people out
nature-gov-204.text: Property prices near New York's High Line, an old rail line turned into a park, rose by 35%. Near Chicago's Bloomingdale Trail, the rise was 13.8% to 48.2%. Cleaner, greener neighborhoods become more desirable, and that can be a problem for the people who already live there. Environmental gentrification is the process by which cleaning up pollution or adding green amenities raises property values and draws wealthier residents into a formerly polluted or neglected area. The amenities include parks, green roofs, gardens and energy-efficient buildings. The mechanism is supply and demand. Green spaces tend to raise housing prices when there is too little housing to meet demand. Rising rents can push low-income households out physically. Long-time residents can also be displaced culturally, socially and politically, even if they stay. The same pattern follows cleanup of toxic Superfund sites. Wealthier, better-educated newcomers tend to move in while earlier residents are slowly priced out. Even measures against urban heat, such as green walls and roofs, can trigger it. Sieg and colleagues first named the process in 2004, joining two older topics: gentrification and environmental justice.

nature-gov-167.title: Environmental defenders: risking life for land
nature-gov-167.text: On average, three environmental defenders are killed every week. For each one killed, up to one hundred more are intimidated, arrested or harassed. Global Witness counted 1,922 murders in 57 countries between 2002 and 2019, about a third of them Indigenous people. An environmental defender is a person or group protecting the environment from harms such as mining, waste dumping, infrastructure projects or land seizure. In 2019 the UN Human Rights Council unanimously recognized their importance. The Environmental Justice Atlas documents over 3500 conflicts, and Indigenous people are involved in 41% of them. Successful campaigns usually combine many non-violent tactics, and 26.7% of reported campaigns ended with the project canceled. Many conflicts arise from renewable energy or conservation projects, with hydroelectric dams the most frequent cause. The 1998 Aarhus Convention gives individuals rights to information, participation and justice. The label itself is disputed. It lumps together very different groups, many of whom do not call themselves defenders.

nature-gov-180.title: Free, prior and informed consent
nature-gov-180.text: A UN declaration, described in {{ref:nature-gov-183}}, states that no Indigenous people may be relocated without their free, prior and informed consent. The principle says an Indigenous people must be consulted, from the ground up, before development starts on its ancestral land or uses resources in its territory. Free means no coercion or bribery. Prior means consent is sought well before work begins. Informed means people learn the project's nature, size, pace and duration. The Philippines' Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997 was the first national law to include it. It has been widely applied in REDD+ forest projects, and UN-REDD issued mandatory guidelines in 2013. Definitions differ, though. Many treaties require only consultation, not consent, so Indigenous peoples cannot veto projects. Industry argues a veto could block projects that benefit the public. Others reply that extraction for profit repeats neocolonial patterns.

nature-gov-170.title: Critical environmental justice
nature-gov-170.text: David Pellow created critical environmental justice to question the assumptions and blind spots of earlier studies. Its scholars hold that several forms of inequality work together to drive environmental injustice. It rests on four pillars. The first is intersectionality, the way inequalities of race, class and gender combine. The others are attention to scale in space and time, seeking justice outside the state, and treating all beings as indispensable.

nature-gov-169.title: The three dimensions of environmental justice
nature-gov-169.text: Environmental justice asks for three kinds of fairness. Distributive justice shares benefits like clean water and green space, and burdens like pollution, evenly across communities. Procedural justice gives affected communities information, a voice in policy and access to the courts. Recognition justice respects the distinct cultures and histories of marginalized groups, including Indigenous peoples. Robert Bullard offers another split: procedural, geographic and social equity. Geographic equity asks how close communities live to hazards such as landfills and incinerators.

nature-gov-172.title: Shipping toxic waste to the Global South
nature-gov-172.text: Through the 1980s and 1990s, toxic waste exports from the United States escalated. Rich countries were shifting dangerous waste to the Global South, where weaker rules made disposal cheaper. Many receiving countries lack proper disposal systems, and local people are not told about the hazards. The Khian Sea incident, when Philadelphia incinerator ash was dumped on a Haitian beach, helped bring about the Basel Convention on moving toxic waste across borders.

nature-gov-171.title: Indigenous environmental justice
nature-gov-171.text: For many Indigenous peoples, environmental justice starts from a colonial situation and may aim at decolonization. In the US, Native Americans fall under a separate legal regime. They are citizens of Indigenous nations whose sovereignty rests on treaties, not ethnic minorities. Scholars such as Dina Gilio-Whitaker argue that the usual focus on fair shares assumes land is a commodity. That clashes with many Indigenous worldviews.

nature-gov-212.title: Green imperialism: environmentalism as interference?
nature-gov-212.text: Green imperialism is a critical label for a perceived Western strategy of meddling in developing nations' affairs in the name of the environment. Helge Ole Bergesen used it in 1988 to sum up how Third World elites saw the Brundtland report. The label eco-colonialism first appeared around debt-for-nature swaps from 1989. Malaysia fought European timber boycotts on these grounds, and in 1994 Brazil, India and Singapore opposed linking trade to pollution controls as hidden protectionism. The term is an insult, and many disagree: a 1990s survey found 66% of respondents did not see the swaps as eco-colonialism.

nature-gov-163.title: Who should pay for climate change?
nature-gov-163.text: Three rules compete for deciding who bears the larger costs of climate change. Those who caused most of it should pay. Those most able to pay should pay. Those who benefited most should pay. A 2023 study estimated the top 21 fossil fuel companies would owe $5.4 trillion in climate reparations over 2025–2050. Some cities apply these ideas in adaptation policy. Barcelona, for example, requires 30% of new housing developments to be social housing.

nature-gov-164.title: Climate fairness across generations
nature-gov-164.text: Under current pledges, children born in 2020 will face 2–7 times as many heat waves in their lives as people born in 1960. The generations mainly responsible for climate change are not the ones who will bear most of its damage. One generation's emissions can lock in harm for those that follow. In April 2021, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled on this point. One generation, it said, must not use up much of the carbon budget and leave later ones a drastic burden of cuts.

nature-gov-196.title: Community-based conservation
nature-gov-196.text: More than 20 million people are estimated to have been displaced by fortress conservation. Community-based conservation grew in the 1980s as a reaction, involving local communities in protecting nature instead of pushing them out. In 1975 the IUCN first accepted that traditional ways of life could support conservation. The 2003 World Parks Congress and a 2004 Biodiversity Convention meeting recognized Indigenous peoples and local communities as governors of protected areas. Co-management splits responsibility between the state and communities, blending traditional knowledge with science. Livelihoods include ecotourism, rotational grazing, forest products other than timber, sustainable fisheries and carbon projects. Community-managed lands in parts of Kenya have shown richer soils and more plant growth. The benefits are not always shared fairly. In Madagascar, local elites captured the gains while poorer households lost access to land. Legal recognition of communal ownership of land is essential for lasting success.

nature-gov-214.title: Territories of life: Indigenous and community conserved areas
nature-gov-214.text: Indigenous and community conserved areas are said to cover as much land as government protected areas. Yet tens of thousands of these sites lack official recognition. They are territories governed, managed and conserved in practice by Indigenous peoples or local communities, with clear benefits for biological and cultural diversity. Since about 2020 they are also called "territories of life." Three features mark one. A community has a strong bond with a place and leads its management. Conservation results follow even when conservation is not the aim. The 2003 IUCN World Parks Congress defined them as places with significant biodiversity that communities conserve voluntarily, through customary law or other means. They may or may not count as formal protected areas. At the 2010 Biodiversity Convention meeting in Nagoya, countries were invited to recognize them. Threats include mining, logging and state takeovers of community land for official reserves.

nature-gov-213.title: Harmony with Nature
nature-gov-213.text: Ahead of a 2012 UN conference in Rio, Bolivia made a bold claim. Nature, it argued, has rights just as humans do, including the right to exist and renew itself. Harmony with Nature is the principle behind that claim: a friendly, holistic coexistence between people and the natural world. It appears mainly in debates on sustainable development and the rights of nature. The United Nations created a Harmony with Nature program in 2009, and Bolivian support led to further resolutions. Bolivia's proposal also called GDP an inadequate measure of well-being and asked for indicators of environmental destruction.

nature-gov-226.title: A patent treaty for genes and traditional knowledge
nature-gov-226.text: After more than two decades of talks, WIPO members concluded a treaty in Geneva on 24 May 2024. Known as GRATK, it requires patent applicants to disclose when an invention is based on genetic resources or the traditional knowledge tied to them. That disclosure indirectly fights biopiracy and supports benefit-sharing rules. It is the first WIPO treaty with provisions written specifically for Indigenous peoples and local communities. It takes effect three months after 15 countries ratify or accede, and 44 countries had signed by May 2025.

nature-gov-177.title: Six facets of traditional ecological knowledge
nature-gov-177.text: Nicholas Houde broke traditional ecological knowledge into six parts. Factual observations are long-term general observations, checked against other knowledge holders' accounts. Management systems cover practices such as pest control, growing several crops together, and judging the state of resources. Then come past and current uses, and ethics and values, which keep exploitation in check. The last two are culture and identity, and cosmology, a people's view of how the world is ordered.

nature-gov-178.title: Cultural burning: fire as a tool and a practice
nature-gov-178.text: Colonists in California banned Indigenous burning in the late 1700s to early 1800s. Decades of fire exclusion followed. Cultural burning is traditional controlled burning that Indigenous peoples use to manage land and as a spiritual practice. The Karuk and Yurok Tribes of California have revived it on their ancestral lands, to cut wildfire risk and restore depleted resources. In Australia, an Indigenous nation that regained land brought back its traditional burning too.

nature-gov-210.title: Neo-extractivism: mining for social programs
nature-gov-210.text: Under Ecuador's Correa government, which expanded oil and mining, poverty fell by 37% and extreme poverty by 49%. That is the promise of neo-extractivism, a model in which governments take more control of resource extraction and its revenue to fund social programs. It spread mainly among Latin America's left-leaning "Pink Tide" governments during the commodity boom of the early 2000s. States rewrite contracts, raise export taxes and push state ownership, while the economy still runs on exports. Critics say tying welfare to commodity sales leaves it exposed to price drops and concentrates power in presidents' hands.

nature-gov-218.title: Land rights: security, not just access
nature-gov-218.text: Being allowed onto land is not the same as having rights to it. Someone with only access can be expelled whenever the owner chooses, which makes life financially insecure. Land rights are the ability to obtain, use and hold land freely, so long as others' rights are respected. Land law sets the rules on ownership. Land rights describe how far society accepts that ownership in practice. UN research finds that rural landlessness strongly predicts poverty and hunger. Customs often bar women from inheriting or buying land, leaving them dependent on male relatives even when they farm it.

nature-gov-200.title: Putting a number on ecological debt
nature-gov-200.text: How much might rich countries owe? Most attempts compare each country's emissions with its fair share per person. In 2000, Neumayer calculated a "historical emissions debt": the gap between a country's actual past emissions and an equal per-person share. Matthews's 2015 method compares the warming each country has caused since 1960 with its share of world population. A "modified equal shares" approach weights shares by each country's basic needs. In principle, a money value could add up the outside costs of past extraction and the pollution poor countries bear from rich countries' consumption.

nature-gov-192.title: The Hoodia case: the San people get a share
nature-gov-192.text: The San people of southern Africa long used the Hoodia plant. In 1996, South Africa's CSIR research council isolated a weight-loss molecule from it, P57, and the patent rights were sold to Pfizer and Phytopharm. The San demanded restitution. A confidential benefit-sharing deal gave them royalties, knowledge exchange and jobs.

nature-gov-191.title: The neem tree fights back
nature-gov-191.text: Indian farmers have used extracts of the neem tree for around 2,000 years, against pests and fungi. In 1994, the company W.R. Grace patented a neem oil antifungal spray anyway. The challenge to such US and European patents became a landmark. The European Patent Office overturned the patent in 2000. The neem tree became a symbol of resistance to corporate control of Indigenous knowledge.
